newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony set to end Nintendo mastery in game market.
newsitem.headline: Sony set to end Nintendo mastery in game market.

text.p: Riding high on extremely strong sales of its cutting-edge PlayStation game console, Sony Corp is seen replacing Nintendo Co Ltd as the king of the home videogame market, analysts say.

Sony Computer Entertainment Inc, a Sony unit, said on Thursday that net sales of PlayStations and its software will reach 650 billion yen ($5.28 billion) in the business year to next March 31, up from 400 billion yen ($3.25 billion) in the previous year.

Although Nintendo has not yet announced its earnings forecast, analysts predict the company's group sales will total some 460 billion yen ($3.73 billion), up from an estimated 418 billion yen ($3.39 billion) in 1996/97.
Nintendo is due to unveil its results for the last business year and its forecasts for this year on May 13.
Sony Computer forecast that worldwide shipments of its 32-bit game machine will total 18 million units in 1997/98, up from estimated shipments of 8.9 million in 1996/97.

A spokesman for Sony Computer said: "The shipments in the current business year will double from last year as demand in all of the three major markets, namely the U.S., Europe and Japan, is expected to expand very rapidly."
Nintendo, meanwhile, plans to ship 12 million units of its 64-bit game machine globally this business year, up from 6.12 million in the previous year.
A Nintendo spokesman shrugged off its arch rival's rapid growth and stressed that its 64-bit game machine, Nintendo64, and PlayStation, which is 32-bit, are different in quality.
The 64-bit game machine has more data-processing capacity and is smarter and faster than the current mainstay 32-bit ones, he said.
"We believe that offering a top-quality game machine and software is essential to keep the market booming," he said.
Analysts said Nintendo would see firm growth in its earnings this year, as sales of the Nintendo64 and software are expected to be strong, especially overseas.

"An increase in sales of software, which have higher margins than game machines, will help the company's profits grow in the current business year," said Yutaka Sugiyama, an analyst at UBS Securities Ltd.
He said Nintendo might sell more than 40 million units of software in 1997/98, up from 16.6 million in 1996/97.
Naoko Ito, an analyst at Goldman Sachs (Japan), said Nintendo would be able to launch a number of game titles which would augment sales of its game machines.

But she said the company's global sales target of 12 million units for 1997/98 may be too high as it faces fierce competition from PlayStation. She said worldwide sales of Nintendo64 will likely total 10 million units.

Ito said the company's operating profit will likely rise 50 percent in 1997/98, although she said it is unlikely that the profit will be boosted by the yen's further retreat against the dollar as it had been in the previous business year.
Ito predicted the company will post a parent current profit of 160.0 billion yen ($1.30 billion) and a group current profit of 183.6 billion yen ($1.49 billion) in 1997/98.
Sugiyama of UBS Securities said Nintendo will likely post a parent current profit of 110 billion yen ($894 million) and a group current profit of 120 billion yen ($975 million).
The analysts said their forecasts of business results for 1996/97 are in line with Nintendo's earnings forecast revisions announced last month.

Nintendo said on April 7 that it saw parent sales of 345.4 billion yen ($2.80 billion) in 1996/97 and current profit of 100.0 billion yen ($813 million). On a group basis, it saw sales of 418 billion yen ($3.39 billion) and current profit of 108.0 billion yen ($878 million). ($1=123 yen)
